text: Tonight, you'll flip a switch, and your whole room will fill with light.
No smoke. No smell. No fire.
But for almost all of human history, when the sun went down, the world went dark.
So how did people see at night?
Rewind seventeen thousand years.
Deep inside Lascaux Cave in France, people painted horses and bulls on the walls, in total darkness.
To do that, they needed light.
Archaeologists found more than a hundred stone lamps in that cave.
They were simple. A hollow stone, a lump of animal fat, and a wick of moss or juniper.
It gave about as much light as a single candle.
Then came clay.
Across the ancient world, people filled small clay lamps with olive oil or animal fat.
The Romans made them by the million, like cheap plastic today.
But light still cost money.
Most candles were made from tallow, which is melted animal fat. They smoked, and they stank.
Beeswax burned clean and bright, but it was so expensive that mostly churches and the rich could use it.
And here's the strange part.
Fire at night was also a danger. One fallen candle could burn down a whole wooden town.
So in medieval Europe, a bell rang every evening, telling people to cover their fires.
In French, cover fire was couvre-feu.
And that's where we get the English word curfew.
Then, in eighteen oh seven, Pall Mall in London became the first street lit by gas lamps.
For the first time, a city stayed bright after dark.
And in eighteen seventy-nine, Thomas Edison's team made a light bulb that could glow for many hours.
Fat. Oil. Wax. Gas. Electricity.
Every step pushed the darkness a little further back.
So tonight, when you flip that switch, remember.
You're holding a fire that burned for seventeen thousand years, finally tamed inside a tiny glass bulb.
